note: Mary's accuracy record. One entry each time her number can be compared against a number a human produced or accepted. This is the ONLY ground truth she has today - the Estimating Log's W/L column is 93% empty (325 jobs, 3 marked won), so 'did we win' cannot be answered from it yet. Outcomes captured on the hub fill that gap from today forward; see data/outcomes (D1 table) and scripts/mary_scoreboard.py.
how_to_add: Whenever you price something that a human also priced - an audit, a re-price, a benchmark that a supplier return later answers - add an entry. mary_estimate is YOUR number, actual is theirs, basis says what theirs was. Never guess either; leave the entry out if you cannot source both. ALSO STATE 'basis_type' - these entries are NOT all measuring the same thing and should not be averaged blind. Most compare Mary's SELL against the SELL Fenster actually issued; St Mary's compares a register benchmark against a supplier's COST. Group before you quote an accuracy figure.

entries.job: Greenfields Respite Barnstaple
entries.basis: Mary's house-format doc (register medians + template adders) vs the manually priced quote Fenster actually sent on 20/07
entries.lesson: Full-height screens must be priced as curtain walling, not as windows. Register alu-door medians badly undercook SMA Smart Wall doorsets. Liniar uPVC live rates run 8-15% below register medians.

entries.job: SM5 Wexham SEND Bungalow
entries.basis: Mary's benchmark aluminium estimate (BSW register medians) against the pricing document Fenster ISSUED to SM5 Developments on 29/07/2026 12:22, FAO Ryan Steadman - GBP 20,563.57 ex VAT, built off BSW Sheerline QT253300 with Bellview 0000000475 doors at 15%. History of this entry: logged 24/07 as issued, corrected 28/07 to 'priced but never sent' when Adam said so, and now genuinely issued - verified against the sent attachment, which differs from the 24/07 version by exactly one cell, the date. So this is at last a clean benchmark-vs-issued point.
entries.lesson: Live Sheerline Prestige runs ~10% above register alu medians, and this benchmark predated the system-depth coupling correction, so the gap on a correctly-built job would be wider than -9.5%. NOTE THE ISSUED FIGURE IS ITSELF SHORT: BSW added GBP 143.01 of restrictors 41 minutes before the send and it never reached the document, so the sell rests on a supply cost we no longer have. When you compare against an issued number, check the supplier quote behind it is still the current one.

entries.job: Filwood Broadway
entries.basis: Mary: Aplus register medians + spec uplift, quoted as contractors provisional sums. Actual: the client quote issued from the job folder (Stepnell - BCC Filwood Broadway Pricing.xlsx)

entries.job: Brocks Hill
entries.basis: Mary: budget/fallback from a blank-rate BoQ, no drawings or supplier quotes. Actual: the client quote issued from the job folder (SMD - Brocks Hill Phase 2 Teaching Block Pricing.xlsx)
entries.lesson: Same 37 units both sides, so this is a clean read on the fallback rates: +18.7% over the supplier-backed number (ex mastic/EPDM, 106,395.48 v 93,673.34). Fallback material rates run high on aluminium. BUT the comparison only holds because BOTH numbers priced the same BoQ - and the BoQ itself omits 7 external doors that are on the architect's door schedule (Type E.01 5no steel sports hall escape, Type E.03 2no louvred plant room) and one Type E.05 window. Neither figure is the job. The real lesson is that agreeing with a bill is not the same as being right: check the schedules before treating a BoQ as the scope.

entries.job: St Mary's Refurbishment, Merthyr Tydfil
entries.basis: Register medians via mary_pricing.find_rate for the 31 Sheerline Prestige casement types (98 units, 160.36 m2), against BSW QT252799's own frame prices for exactly the same units. The engine applied the MEASURED bsw factor 1.056 from learned-rates.json, not the CALIBRATION Sheerline 1.10 - derived_factors() supersedes CALIBRATION, so on a BSW Sheerline job the Sheerline correction never fires. Uncorrected the register would have given GBP 63,011.59 (+4.4%); with the Sheerline 1.10 instead it would have been GBP 69,312.75 (+14.8%).
entries.lesson: THE AGGREGATE IS AN ACCIDENT OF MIX. Whole-job error is only +4.4% uncorrected because large band errors cancel: <1.5m2 is -35.5% (register UNDER-prices small units - actual GBP 697/m2 against a median of GBP 450), 1.5-3m2 is -1.2% (excellent), 3-6m2 is +37.5% and >6m2 is +35.2% (register OVER-prices large units). Per type the spread is -43.6% to +46.9% and only 15 of 31 land within +/-20%. So the register is a good whole-package predictor ONLY where the unit mix is broad, and a poor per-element one outside the 1.5-3m2 band. Both available corrections make this job worse, not better - the raw median was closest. One job is not enough to move a factor built on 273 lines, so nothing in the engine was changed; the band structure, not the supplier factor, is what looks wrong.

entries.job: Georgie's (formerly Rosebank)
entries.basis: Mary's 27/07 register benchmark for the scope no supplier had quoted - 7 doors on BSW glazed-door medians (GBP 8,021) plus the 16.23 m2 CW01+D03+CW02 run on the house GBP 850/m2 curtain-walling template (GBP 13,795) - against the supplier returns that landed 28/07: Bellview 0000000513 GBP 20,861.92 net of 15% (CW run + D01 + D04 + D05-D08) plus BSW QT253508 GBP 2,381.70 (D02 patio). Identical scope both sides.
entries.lesson: The benchmark was labelled 'a floor and not a price' and it was one, by 6.1% - the first entry where the stated direction held. But the margin is flattered: the benchmark was called low because it carried no panic hardware, pivot/concealed-closer set or master-key suiting, and the actual return turned out to carry almost none of that either (4 of 6 required BS EN 1125 devices absent, no suiting at all). So -6.1% is the gap between two prices that BOTH omit the hardware, not the gap to a compliant one. When you flag a benchmark as a floor because of missing content, check the supplier return actually contains that content before treating the comparison as closed.

entries.job: Redditch Library BLBS0956
entries.client: Pride Developments (for Worcestershire CC via Gleeds)
entries.basis_type: benchmark SELL vs competitor's tendered SELL
entries.basis: Identical take-off both sides - Gleeds' blank pricing schedule (pack p77) and Joedan's Appendix 2 schedule (p150) are the same 43 rows, same sizes, same configurations, so quantity error is zero and the whole difference is rate. Mary: learned/register benchmarks through mary_pricing, frames GBP 60,551.26 + template code adders GBP 19,875.00 + fit labour GBP 7,670.00 + solar-control glass premium GBP 1,814.51. Joedan JCQ.9727, 23/03/2026, Nathan Swenson: GBP 90,687.17 ex VAT gross of 2.5% MCD, so GBP 88,419.99 net to a main contractor. A NEW KIND OF ENTRY - the first where the comparator is a competitor's tendered price for the same building rather than Fenster's own issued quote or a supplier return.
entries.lesson: -0.9% against Joedan's gross and +1.7% against their net, and the closeness is NOT the finding - it is two errors pointing opposite ways and cancelling. THE COMPARISON IS NOT LIKE FOR LIKE: Joedan's figure INCLUDES strip-out of the existing windows (their cl.12) and Mary's excludes it because no strip-out rate exists anywhere in Fenster's records. So on identical scope Fenster is already ABOVE Joedan by the whole cost of stripping 43 openings out of an occupied library, before anything else. Against that, 62% of this job's value sits in the 3-6 m2 band where St Mary's measured the register +37.5% high, and applying the St Mary's band corrections to the supply component alone gives GBP 79,047.55, or -12.8% against Joedan. TWO LESSONS. First, when a benchmark lands within 1% of a real price, check what each number contains before believing it - here the agreement was an accident. Second, this is the sixth of seven entries and the fifth to run high, which is now a settled pattern rather than a run: whatever the aggregate says, a 3-6 m2-weighted job should be expected high and said so on the face of the document.

entries.job: Redditch Library BLBS0956 - engine vs BSW QT250834 (Severn Trent)
entries.basis_type: benchmark COST vs supplier COST, per size band
entries.basis: Not a whole-job comparison - a BAND comparison, which is the useful kind. BSW quotation QT250834, 15/06/2026, quoted to Fenster for PRIDE DEVELOPMENTS' Severn Trent job: Sheerline Prestige aluminium casements, factory glazed, trickle vents, shootbolt locking, cills and couplers. Six lines, 27 units, 72.578 m2, Total Nett Ex VAT GBP 34,902.35, which the extracted lines reconcile to exactly. Unit rates GBP 629.63/m2 at 1.440 m2 down to GBP 336.78/m2 at 6.750 m2 fit rate = 721.47 x area^-0.4093 with R2 = 0.9934. Redditch's 43 items re-priced on that curve give GBP 56,995.38 of frame supply against the engine's GBP 60,551.26. Same supplier, same client, six weeks old, same product family, and the size range brackets Redditch's.
entries.lesson_followup_2026_07_29: The last line of this lesson - that the code adder is a fixed sum per unit and so quietly halves margin on big units - turns out to be only half the story. The estimator had already noticed and had already been correcting for it by hand; nobody had written the correction down. Measured across all 30 sent pricing documents, the money in the unit rate over and above Frames is the code value x 75% almost exactly below 6 m2 (median x1.00 against the template adder, n=453 lines) and the code value x 125% above 6 m2 (median x1.250, n=60, nine different jobs). So the template's fixed adder is right where it was set, and wrong only past 6 m2, where the estimator silently switches to 125%. That is now in the engine as ADDER_FACTOR_LARGE - see the entry of 2026-07-29.
entries.lesson: THE BAND STRUCTURE IS NOW EVIDENCED TWICE, INDEPENDENTLY, AND IT IS THE REAL FINDING - the -5.9% whole-job number is not. Engine error by band (positive = engine sits above the real price): under 1.5 m2, St Mary's -35.5% against Severn Trent -38.9%; 1.5-3 m2, -1.2% against -20.4%; 3-6 m2, +37.5% against +18.1%; over 6 m2, +35.2% against +34.1%. Two different jobs, different suppliers, different dates, agreeing within four points on the small band and within one point on the large band. The register UNDER-prices small units by roughly a third and OVER-prices large ones by roughly a third, and on a broad mix those errors cancel - which is exactly why whole-job accuracy has looked better than per-element accuracy all along. St Mary's said this from one job and it was reasonable to hold it lightly; it should not be held lightly any more. TWO CAVEATS THAT BOTH PUSH THE COMPARATOR HIGH, so the engine's over-pricing on the big bands is if anything understated here: the Severn Trent job is 3005 Wine Red metallic, a premium colour, and its outer pane is 6.8 laminated rather than 4mm toughened. AND A SEPARATE ONE WORTH ITS OWN LINE: the house template's code adder is a FIXED SUM PER UNIT, so margin falls as units grow - 50.7% of the frame line under 1.5 m2, 19.0% at 3-6 m2, 12.2% over 6 m2. Redditch averages 3.18 m2 and earns 24.7%; Crestwood Park averaged 1.29 m2 and earned 42.9%. Nobody had noticed that the template quietly prices big-unit work at half the margin of small-unit work.

entries.job: Adder factor above 6 m2 - engine change, not a job
entries.basis_type: engine change, measured on sent SELL and holdout-tested
entries.basis: Not a single-job comparison. For every priced line in all 30 back-testable sent quotes, the non-Frames money in the unit rate (unit_rate - frames) was divided by the product's CODE_VALUE. Below 6 m2 that ratio is 0.75 - the template factor - with a median of x1.00 against the template adder in every band and every code (n=453). Above 6 m2 the median is 1.250 exactly (n=60 lines, 9 jobs). Pooled it is x1.67 against the 75% adder; excluding the three Brandon Estate documents, which are large enough to dominate any money-weighted figure, it is still x1.67; and the median of the nine per-job medians is x1.67. Split 6-8 / 8-12 / 12+ m2 the engine error was flat (-16.1%, -17.8%, -10.9%), so this is a step at 6 m2 and not a slope - the band boundary is in the right place.
entries.lesson_band_answer_2026_07_29: This entry also answers the question St Mary's and Severn Trent left open - whether the band structure itself is wrong. It is, but NOT in the way those two jobs suggested. St Mary's small-runs-low / large-runs-high pattern DOES NOT GENERALISE: pooled across all 30 sent quotes the engine's band errors were -5.2% (<1.5m2), +0.1% (1.5-3), -4.3% (3-6) and -17.3% (>6). Small does not run low across the corpus, and large ran low, not high. The real fault in the >6m2 band was the adder, not the band, and once that was fixed the band error went to -3.3%. What IS wrong with the structure is subtler: the learned rates were being keyed on the REGISTER's bands (1.5/3/6), which the register's own category strings fix and which nobody had ever asked to suit the mined data. Re-keyed on 2/5 they are better on all three folds. See the entry below.
entries.lesson: THE ESTIMATOR TAKES THE CODE VALUE AT 125%, NOT 75%, ONCE A UNIT PASSES 6 m2, and has been doing it by hand all along. The commercial reason is that a unit over 6 m2 is a coupled screen and not a single leaf: extra mullions, transoms, sealing and glass that a per-unit code value was never sized for. This is the estimator's own rule read back off what they charged, so it is not a fudge factor - which is why it is implemented as a second ADDER_FACTOR rather than as a CALIBRATION entry. HOW IT WAS TESTED, because the 1.25 was read off all 30 documents and scoring it on those same 30 would prove nothing: the 1.25 was re-derived from the 20 training jobs alone (giving 1.366, n=33) and, separately, from the 10 holdout jobs alone - which had never been used to fit it - giving 1.250 exactly, n=27. An independent half of the data reproducing the constant to three figures is much stronger evidence than the aggregate error move, which is small (holdout mean abs 14.5% -> 14.3%) only because just 3 of the 10 holdout jobs carry meaningful large-unit money. On those three the change is large and right: Filwood -7.4% -> +3.6% and Elkins Brandon -9.5% -> -2.7%. Full scan: median abs 12.7% -> 10.4%, within 10% 13/30 -> 14/30, bias -7.2% -> -5.2%. AND A WARNING FOR WHOEVER READS THIS NEXT: do NOT read the earlier band entries as contradicting this one. St Mary's and Severn Trent measured the FRAME SUPPLY RATE against a supplier's COST and found the register over-prices big units by about a third. This measures the WHOLE UNIT RATE against Fenster's own SELL and finds the engine under-priced big units by 17.3%. Both are true and they are about different components - the supply rate and the adder. Averaging them, or treating one as refuting the other, would be a mistake.

entries.job: Learned rates get their own size bands - engine change, not a job
entries.basis: The learned rates mined from the Frames column were keyed on band_of(), which exists to match the REGISTER's category strings - 'aluminium casement window, glazed [1.5-3m2]'. Those boundaries are a property of a 15,551-line supplier-quote register nobody chose them for, and the mined data was never asked whether they suited it. Seven structures were tried, each re-learned from the training jobs and scored on jobs never seen. Boundaries at 2 and 5 m2 beat 1.5/3/6 on all three folds: mean abs 14.3/16.5/17.9 -> 11.7/14.1/16.5, mean of folds 16.2% -> 14.1%, median 13.0% -> 9.8%, with identical line counts and zero skipped lines in both arms so the comparison is like for like.
entries.lesson: TWO THINGS, AND THE SECOND MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIRST. First: the register's bands are not the mined data's bands, and there was never a reason they should be. band_of() now serves the register only, and learned_band_of() serves the learned rates, which is the split that should have existed from the start. Second, and this is the one to remember: MAKING THE BANDS FINER MADE THE ENGINE WORSE, clearly - adding a boundary at 10 m2 took mean abs from 13.5% to 17.6% on the same lines. There are only 513 mined lines, and every extra band divides them until buckets fall under MIN_LEARNED_N and drop through to the register, which is the weaker evidence. The instinct on seeing band error is to add bands; on this corpus that is exactly backwards, and the next person to look should not spend the hour finding it out again. A THIRD LESSON, ON METHOD: the first version of this test let lines that could not be priced silently drop out of the score instead of being priced badly. The coarsest structure then won by simply dropping the hardest lines, and it looked like a 5-point improvement. Held to a constant line set it was worth nothing. And 1.5/4 won a single fold by 0.9 points and lost the other two - had only one fold been run it would have shipped. Any future band claim needs a constant line set and all three folds.

entries.job: Grange Hill Methodist Church
entries.basis_type: Mary benchmark SELL vs supplier-backed SELL through the same engine
entries.basis: 24/07 benchmark GBP 27,560.07: two glazed elevations taken as single rectangles off 1:100 drawings with no schedule, priced on the curtain-walling convention (850 supply + 150 labour per m2). 29/07 supplier-backed GBP 37,278.59: BSW quotes 0000000520 (doors, SMA Smart Wall, GBP 13,354.08 Grand Total Net after 15%) and QT253562 (windows, Sheerline Prestige, GBP 9,477.01 already net), buy GBP 22,831.09, run line by line through mary_pricing. Both figures exclude spec 3.15 and 3.16 and both exclude the operator and manifestation allowances, so the comparison is like for like.
entries.lesson: TWO LARGE ERRORS IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS PRODUCED A PLAUSIBLE TOTAL. The rate was roughly double and the area roughly a third, and -26.1% is what was left after they cancelled. Separately they are much worse than that: my CW convention priced at about GBP 1,000/m2 sell where BSW sell the same work at GBP 598/m2, and I measured 23.49 m2 against their 62.33 m2. (1) The CW convention overstates a domestic-scale gabled screen that a supplier will actually build as coupled casements over a door element - check how the thing will be MADE before applying 850/150. (2) Taking an elevation as one rectangle at door-plus-a-bit height understates it whenever the spec says the glazing runs to the underside of a pitched roof. GH007 puts eaves at 2800 and the ridge at 5183; I used 2400 on the west and 2747 on the south. BSW's own west door element is 4588 x 2100, which leaves only 1.4 m2 above it in my take-off for glazing the spec says must reach the ceiling - that alone shows my height was wrong. NOTE THE AREA IS NOT YET AGREED: BSW say 'I have rescaled the south elevation as take off provided was incorrect' and sent no setting-out drawing, and their south width of 5900 is within 100mm of the chapel's 5800 - the element they excluded. Reconcile before ordering.
entries.size_band_note: Weighted to large units. Contradicts the earlier '+35% on >6m2' reading - here the register was not the problem, the take-off and the convention were.

entries.job: Grange Hill Methodist Church (WD001 tender return)
entries.basis_type: Mary supplier-backed SELL vs the estimator's supplier-backed SELL, same two supplier quotes
entries.basis: Both figures are built on the same buy: Bellview 0000000520 doors and BSW QT253562 windows, 29/07/2026. Mine ran all 16 units through mary_pricing and came to GBP 37,278.59 (before GBP 3,250 of house allowances for the 3.13.1 operator and 3.11.2 manifestations, which are excluded from both sides of this comparison). Gintare's pricing document, sent to Adam 13:10 the same day, came to GBP 39,006.77. NOT PERFECTLY LIKE FOR LIKE: she prices 15 units, I priced 16 - she schedules seven 1200x1183 windows where BSW quote eight, which is the GBP 419.32 discrepancy reported to Adam. So she is 4.4% above me on ONE FEWER UNIT; on equal units the gap is wider still.
entries.lesson: FIRST TIME I HAVE COME IN LOW AGAINST A HUMAN, and it is the first comparison where both sides were supplier-backed rather than one being a register benchmark. The five earlier points are four high and one low with a mean bias of +10.4%, and every high one compared a REGISTER benchmark against a real sell. Take the register out and the bias does not survive: when the supply price is the supplier's own, what differs is only the house adder and labour, and there the estimator is more generous than the engine's code mapping. My code assignment reproduces GBP 37,278.59 exactly but is not unique - reasonable alternative codes span about GBP 1,160 (3%) on this job, which is the real resolution of a template that prices by product code rather than by unit. DO NOT QUOTE AN ENGINE FIGURE TO THREE DECIMAL PLACES AS IF IT WERE THE ONLY ONE THE TEMPLATE GIVES. And the wider lesson has nothing to do with arithmetic: I should not have produced a second number at all. quote_send_dates.py would have shown the estimator's pack existed.
entries.size_band_note: Not a size-band finding. Both sides carry the identical unit mix apart from the one disputed 1200x1183, so the difference is entirely in code adders and labour.

entries.job: ADDER_FACTOR_LARGE re-measured directly - the 1.25 is a fudge, not the estimator's rule
entries.basis_type: engine change: constant KEPT, stated reason CORRECTED, 3-fold cross-validated
entries.basis: The 29/07 entry below derived ADDER_FACTOR_LARGE = 1.25 from (unit_rate - frames) / CODE_VALUE on lines over 6 m2. That quantity is NOT the adder. The engine's learned rate is mined from the Frames column alone, so unit_rate - frames contains the adder PLUS Glass PLUS Additional PLUS CW. scripts/mary_quote_audit.py reads all four component columns, which makes the adder directly measurable as unit_rate - (frames + glass + additional + cw). Measured that way over 508 lines with a full build-up: the factor is 0.750 in EVERY band, including above 6 m2. On the 28 large-unit lines outside the three Brandon Estate documents, 26 (93%) sit on exactly 0.75 and ZERO sit on 1.25. The Brandon documents are excluded on a property of the line and not by name - their frames+glass+additional+cw EXCEEDS their own unit rate, giving factors of -3.6 to -5.8, so those columns cannot be per-unit money there.
entries.lesson: THE 1.25 IS ARITHMETIC, NOT A HABIT. The median of glass+additional+cw on a large unit is GBP 1,000.00 and the median large unit is a DAD with a code value of 2,000, so charging that money to the code value gives 0.75 + 1000/2000 = 1.25 exactly. THE CONSTANT STAYS ANYWAY, and this is the part that matters for anyone tempted to revert it: it earns its place on jobs it has not seen. Three folds, constant line set, rates re-mined per fold - mean abs 13.88 at 1.25 against 14.46 at 0.75, winning two folds of three. So it is kept as an ADMITTED FUDGE for money the engine does not model, and the claim that the estimator does this by hand is withdrawn. AND THE PRINCIPLED FIX IS WORSE, which is worth having as a closed question: modelling the extras as a flat learned sum above 6 m2 with the adder back at 0.75 - learned correctly at GBP 1,000/600/1,000 across the three folds once non-reconciling lines are dropped - scores 14.73, worse than either arm. The extras are scope items that vary, not a constant. THE METHOD LESSON IS THE BIGGEST ONE. The 29/07 entry treated 'an independent half of the data reproduced the constant to three figures' as much stronger evidence than the error move. It is not, when the constant comes from a systematic measurement confound: the confound reproduces in every split, so a holdout cannot see it. A holdout tests whether a number generalises, never whether it measures what its name says. The only thing that caught this was measuring the same quantity a second way.
entries.size_band_note: Does not disturb the 29/07 learned-rate band finding (boundaries at 2 and 5), which was cross-validated on a different quantity and stands.

entries.job: The engine can now see Glass and Additional - supply mined from the whole build-up, and the 1.25 fudge retired
entries.client: (all 29 scored pricing documents; CW finding across 65)
entries.basis_type: engine change: KEPT, decided on leave-one-out over all 29 documents
entries.basis: Two findings, the second only possible because of the first. (1) THE CW COLUMN IS A WORKING COLUMN. 156 of 508 priced lines had frames+glass+additional+cw exceeding their own unit rate, which the entry below set aside as the three Brandon Estate documents being 'not per-unit money'. It is not a Brandon property: it is 156 lines across 9 documents, and on every single one of them the CW cell equals area x GBP 850.00 - CW_SUPPLY_M2 - to within 1%, median GBP 850.00/m2 exactly. It is the estimator asking 'what would this opening cost as curtain walling instead', parked in a spare column next to CW LABOUR and CW SQM. Oldswinford row 9 proves it: Frames 1,003.70 + Additional 210.00 + LAW adder 487.50 = 1,701.20, the unit rate to the penny, while the CW cell says 2,041.67 and CW SQM says 2.40. Excluding it takes the build-up reconciliation from 352/508 lines to 495/508. (2) SO THE DOCUMENT'S ARITHMETIC IS frames + glass + additional + 0.75 x code_value, and the engine's learned rate was mined from the Frames column ALONE - leaving Glass and Additional as money it had no term for anywhere: 20.4% of supply above 6 m2, 9.3% at 2-3 m2. Mining the whole build-up per code and per band (mary_backtest.supply_money) lets ADDER_FACTOR_LARGE go back to a flat 0.75.
entries.lesson: THE FUDGE AND THE MISSING TERM WERE THE SAME MONEY, and the proof is that keeping both is the worst option of the four. Arms scored leave-one-out: whole build-up with 0.75 flat 13.24%; Frames only with 1.25 large 14.02%; Frames only with 0.75 flat 14.46%; whole build-up WITH 1.25 large 14.88%, the worst, because it charges the extras twice. The 30/07 entry below had already worked out that the 1.25 was the median GBP 1,000 of extras on a large unit charged to a median code value of 2,000; what it lacked was a way to model the extras instead of standing in for them. Every learned rate moved UP, by 0% to +31%, which is why the bias improved from -4.91% to -1.66%: the engine had been systematically under-pricing because it could not see part of its own supply money. DECIDED ON LEAVE-ONE-OUT, NOT THREE FOLDS. On three positional folds this is 13.88 -> 13.68 with one fold of three won, which is exactly the shape of result that has misled this board twice. Leave-one-out scores all 29 documents on rates mined from the other 28, so no answer depends on where a file sits in the scan order: better on 16 documents, worse on 11, level on 2. AND IT REPAIRED A SUPPLIER FACTOR THAT HAD BEEN REJECTED AS IMPLAUSIBLE. TruFrame measured x0.485 on the Frames-only basis, outside the plausible 0.65-1.55 band, so it was held back unapplied. On the whole build-up it is x0.860 and applies. TruFrame documents put an unusual share of their money in Additional rather than Frames - Trafalgar House prices LPVC frames at GBP 55/m2 against unit rates near GBP 1,700 - so 'TruFrame is half price' was an artefact of which column the money sat in, not a discount. All four suppliers now sit within 0.6% of 1.00 except TruFrame: the estimator's supply per m2 is consistent across suppliers once you look at the whole build-up, which is itself evidence the new basis measures the right thing.

entries.job: THE BAND STRUCTURE IS NOT WRONG - a clean negative on the open question, do not spend the hour again
entries.basis_type: NEGATIVE RESULT - hypothesis tested and rejected, no engine change made
entries.basis: The question carried into 30/07 was: on St Mary's the whole-job error was +4.4% but the register bands were -35.5% (<1.5m2), -1.2% (1.5-3m2), +37.5% (3-6m2) and +35.2% (>6m2), so small runs low and large runs high and the bands cancel out - if that is real across jobs then the band structure itself is wrong and fixing it beats any number of individual rates. Measured two independent ways and it is NOT real. (1) HONEST PER-LINE ERROR BY AREA, all 508 lines, three folds, every line scored on rates mined from other jobs: 0-1m2 +3.7%, 1-1.5 -1.6%, 1.5-2 +5.1%, 2-3 +1.2%, 3-5 +3.2%, 5-6 +30.4% (n=7 only), 6+ +0.9%. Flat, and not monotonic. By the engine's own learned bands: <2m2 +3.0%, 2-5m2 +2.1%, >5m2 +3.8% - uniform to within 1.7 points. (2) ST MARY'S ITSELF NO LONGER SHOWS THE SPREAD: whole job -3.7% with bands -14.2%, +0.2%, -6.3%, +4.0%. The +37.5/-35.5 spread is not there. The whole-job sign has also flipped since 29/07, so part of this is the engine having changed underneath the figure - but the claim that mattered, small-low and large-high, does not survive the archive.
entries.lesson: THE ENGINE ALREADY HAS THE FIXED-PLUS-VARIABLE STRUCTURE THE QUESTION WAS ASKING FOR, and it is in the adder, not the bands. Within a single product code the estimator's raw GBP/m2 really does fall steeply with area - MAW runs 1,149 / 410 / 385 / 309 across the buckets, SAD 954 / 556 / 378, LAW 950 / 420 / 337 - which is what a declining rate curve looks like and is exactly why the hypothesis was plausible. But a declining GBP/m2 is the signature of a fixed cost per opening plus a variable cost per m2, and the template already charges a fixed cost per opening: the code adder, 0.75 x code value, identical whatever the size. On a small SAW that adder is GBP 337.50 against roughly GBP 322 of supply, so more than half the unit rate is already a flat per-unit charge. The bands only ever had to carry the residual variable part, and three of them are enough for that. Splitting them finer was separately tested on 29/07 and was clearly worse, because 508 mined lines will not support more than three buckets before each falls under MIN_LEARNED_N. THE TRANSFERABLE POINT: an aggregate band error is a mix effect and says almost nothing about band boundaries. St Mary's <1.5m2 band was 41 lines of one product and its 3-6m2 band was 3 lines of another, so the two 'bands' were really two products, and the spread was measuring product mix. Always re-measure a per-job band pattern across the whole archive before treating it as structural. THE ONE REAL RESIDUAL: the 5-6m2 bucket is +30.4%, the worst in the archive, on 7 lines. Those sit inside the >5m2 learned band, which wants about GBP 362/m2 at 5-6m2 and more above 6m2 - four of the seven are the Zelltec Crownhill DADs at 5.24m2. Seven lines will not support a band of their own (MIN_LEARNED_N is 6), so this is noted, not fixed.

entries.job: TWO NEGATIVES on the remaining error - repetition buys nothing, and 29 documents will not support a product-factor layer
entries.basis_type: NEGATIVE RESULTS - both hypotheses tested leave-one-out and REJECTED, no engine change made
entries.basis: After the build-up change, leave-one-out leaves six documents above 29% and between them they are 7.3 of the 13.24-point mean, so that is where the error lives. Reading them line by line gives three candidate causes: the product code does not capture the product (CB Refrigeration prices SAD/DAD lines at GBP 881-1,474/m2 against learned 475/668, and the heading rows above them read 'External Steel Door' and 'Internal Steel door' - Strongdoor steel security doors carrying aluminium door codes); repetition (Trafalgar House prices 58 identical 1.92m2 MPVC windows at GBP 108.8/m2 against a learned 221.66, the same shape as Brandon's 2,202 units); and job-level price level (Georgie's windows need GBP 955-1,940/m2, its own median is 1,025 against an archive 400). HYPOTHESIS 1, REPETITION: rejected outright. Ratio of a line's own supply rate to its code+band median against line quantity is 1.035 at qty 1 and 1.000 at qty 41+. Log-log slope -0.0232, R-squared 0.0109 - one percent of the variance - and x0.908 across the whole range from 1 to 64 units. Per job it is slope -0.0193, R-squared 0.0034. Tenbury Close is qty 8 at ratio 2.52, high quantity AND dear, which is the wrong way round. HYPOTHESIS 2, PRODUCT FACTORS FROM THE SECTION HEADING: the signal is real but does not generalise. Headings were extracted and carried down onto the lines beneath them (found on 485 of 486 lines) and measured against the code+band median: 'steel' x1.677 over 9 lines in 3 jobs, 'aluminium sliding sash windows' x3.23, 'fd30 external & communal doors' x2.30, 'internal steel door' x2.22. Learned per fold from a vocabulary fixed in advance, with guards of >=6 lines, >=2 distinct jobs and a plausibility band, it scores 15.03% against a 13.11% baseline - worse on 10 documents, better on 7, within-10 down from 16 to 14. Restricting to product groups that are a MINORITY of their own band, and to steel alone, both give 14.28%. Still worse.

before.note: engine as committed, no product factor

after.note: best guarded product-factor variant - REJECTED, reverted

entries.lesson: A FACTOR MEASURED AS line-rate / band-median IS INVALID TO APPLY WHERE THAT PRODUCT DOMINATES THE BAND, and this is the reusable point. The band median already contains those lines, so the ratio is 1.00 by construction and every deviation from it is noise you then amplify. It shows in the numbers: the keywords that survived the evidence guards were the broad ones sitting at no signal - sheerline x0.970 on 130 lines, comar x1.000 on 82, sma x1.089 on 52, liniar x1.028 on 56 - while the keywords that genuinely separate were too thin to survive (sliding sash 4 lines, fd30 3 lines). Applying near-1.00 factors to well-priced lines is what did the damage: Zelltec Crownhill went +14.6% to +39.9%, Filwood +5.8% to +19.0%. The honest version of this fix is a FINER RATE BUCKET, code|band|product-group, not a multiplicative correction on a contaminated baseline - and 29 documents and 508 lines will not feed it, which is the same wall that stopped finer size bands on 29/07. NOTE THE BIAS MOVED THE RIGHT WAY while the error got worse (-1.88% to -0.71%), so the headings do carry real information; there is just not enough of it. With 9 steel lines in 3 jobs, a fold that drops one of those jobs re-mines a completely different factor. AND THE HEADINGS INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED TWO HAND-TYPED CONSTANTS, which is worth having on its own: the heading 'SMA Smart Wall Aluminium Doors & Screens' measures x1.45 over 11 lines against mary_pricing.CALIBRATION's typed-in 1.45 for Smart Wall, and 'Liniar uPVC Windows & Doors' measures x0.90 over 24 lines against its typed-in 0.90. Both were read off the Greenfields comparison on 22/07 by hand. They are right.

entries.job: THE SUPPLIER CORRECTION WAS MEASURED AND DISCARDED - and two negatives, the heading text and thinning repeated jobs
entries.basis_type: ENGINE CHANGE plus TWO NEGATIVES, all decided leave-one-JOB-out - not comparable with the SELL-vs-SELL entries below, do not average
entries.basis: Third lab run of 30/07. FIRST, A MEASUREMENT FIX THAT MADE THE HONEST NUMBER WORSE: the corpus is 29 documents but 26 JOBS - Brandon Estate is in it three times (Elkins 7,196,696, a COMAR variant 6,184,746, an earlier 11-line version 3,998,687) and Zelltec Crownhill twice. Leaving out one DOCUMENT left other revisions of the same estate in the training set at the same elevations and unit rates, so the engine was shown the answer. Holding out the JOB moves 13.11% to 13.58% and the earlier Brandon revision from +11.5% to +21.3%. The 30/07 content dedup could not see this and was right not to: it matches identical priced lines, and these genuinely differ. THEN THE CHANGE: learn_supplier_factors() measures how dear each supplier runs with code and size held constant and writes it to learned-rates.json, but only find_rate() - the REGISTER path - ever read it. engine_price() returns as soon as it has a learned rate, and all 508 archive lines have one, so the measurement reached nothing. Applying it takes leave-one-JOB-out 13.58% to 13.28% and the three folds 13.51% to 13.20%. The whole gain is TruFrame: 0.859 measured with Trafalgar House held out, 0.910 with Zelltec held out, worth Trafalgar +29.7 to +18.6 and Zelltec +17.2 to +10.8 and +4.7 to -1.3. It is WORSE on 10 documents and better on 8, within-10 falls 16 to 15, and every loss is Aplus, whose factor is 0.894/1.002/1.028 depending on the fold. Gating on per-job agreement is the right fix and scores 13.67% - worse than nothing - because TruFrame has only two jobs, so holding either out leaves one. NEGATIVE 1, THE PRODUCT HEADING. The section heading names the system and the type and the engine has no term for it; measured across the archive the headings separate hard (sliding sash 3.228, fd30 2.302, internal steel 2.222, smart wall 1.492, modeal coupled 0.596). It does not generalise. Eight arms, vocabulary fixed before any factor was read, factors re-mined per fold: best 13.29% against 13.11% baseline, worst 15.86%. The headings that separate hardest are each unique to ONE job and the ones that repeat sit on 1.00 (door 1.000, window 1.000, sheerline 0.970, comar 1.000, upvc 1.004). The board's standing 'steel runs x1.677, worth a code of its own' scores 14.42% and must come off: CB Refrigeration needs it (-32.6% without) and Zelltec does not (+14.6% becomes +39.9%), and both buy Strongdoor steel doors on an aluminium code. NEGATIVE 2, THINNING THE REPEATED JOBS. Mining one document per job costs 0.73 points (13.58 to 14.31) and costs it on unrelated jobs - Brocks Hill -8.0 to -14.9, Oldswinford -16.9 to -23.0. A COMAR re-price of the same elevations is a second real observation, not a duplicate. Capping any one job at 1/6 of a bucket is genuinely ambiguous - mean abs 13.67 worse, but median 6.98 v 7.98, within-10 17 v 16 and the whole-archive figure +5.36% v +6.38% all better - and was rejected because mean abs is the declared decision metric and it went the wrong way. Recorded so a later session can take it up deliberately rather than rediscover it.
entries.lesson: A MONEY-WEIGHTED ACCURACY FIGURE EXISTS NOW AND IT NEEDS ITS WARNING ATTACHED. Whole archive, honest: human 16,036,021 against Mary 17,053,501, +6.34%, money-weighted absolute 7.30%. That is NOT a second opinion on the 13.28% per-document mean - the three Brandon revisions are 89% of the priced money, so the money figure is very nearly a report on one estate, while the per-document mean is pulled by three 1-2 line quotes averaging 29.94% error that are 0.2% of the money. Quote the per-document mean as the headline and the money as the exposure, and never one without the other.

entries.job: FOUR NEGATIVES on the remaining error - quantity, date, MIN_LEARNED_N, coarser bands
entries.basis: leave-one-JOB-out over 29 documents in 26 jobs, the lab's decision metric. Four hypotheses tested, all rejected, NO ENGINE CHANGE MADE - the engine ends the night exactly where it started at 13.28% mean absolute, median 7.92%, bias -2.01%, 15/29 within 10%.
entries.basis_type: NEGATIVE RESULTS - four hypotheses tested leave-one-JOB-out and REJECTED, no engine change made
entries.lesson: QUANTITY. 'A supplier prices a run of one differently from a run of sixty' is true as commerce and is not in this money. Each line's own supply GBP/m2 over the median for its OWN code and band: qty 1 -> 1.035, 5-8 -> 0.957, 41+ -> 1.000. Log-log slope -0.023, R^2 0.0109 over 486 lines; per JOB median R^2 0.0034. A 3.5% effect against errors of 30-50%. THE TRAP: at qty 1 the MEAN ratio is 1.149 against a MEDIAN of 1.035, and the two worst documents in the archive are both single-unit one-line jobs, so the hypothesis fits the worst list perfectly and is still the wrong way round. DATE. Unanswerable here: all 29 documents are 2026, dated 25/03 to 29/07, a span of 0.2 years. It does settle for free that the learned rates need no inflation adjustment to be quoted today. MIN_LEARNED_N. Never tested, and already at its optimum: 3 -> 13.91, 5 -> 13.51, 6 -> 13.28, 8 -> 13.29, 10 -> 13.48. Lowering it is the worse half - a bucket of three lines really is anecdote and the register beats it. COARSER SIZE BANDS. The edges had been tested finer and sideways, never coarser, and the product code already encodes size. One bucket per code scores 19.38% against the current (2.0, 5.0) at 13.28%, so the band does work the code does not.

entries.job: CURTAIN WALLING - the engine could not price it at all, and 8 rows it prices to the penny
entries.basis: leave-one-JOB-out over 29 documents in 26 jobs, the lab's decision metric. BEFORE 13.28% mean abs / median 7.92% / bias -2.01% / 15-29 within 10 / 508 lines. AFTER 12.28% / median 6.86% / bias -1.83% / 17-29 within 10 / 516 lines. --holdout --folds 13.20% -> 12.19%.
entries.basis_type: COVERAGE GAIN, NOT AN ACCURACY GAIN - the denominator changed, 508 lines to 516, and these two figures are NOT the same measurement. Quote them as a pair or not at all. Not one of the 508 lines already priced moved: the learned rate table is byte-identical either side, 18 buckets, sha 41896b6a94ff44ee, verified by running HEAD's learn() and the new one over the same corpus in one process.
entries.lesson: THE ENGINE HAD A CURTAIN-WALLING CONVENTION SINCE 22/07 AND NOTHING COULD REACH IT. read_doc dropped every row whose code was not in CODE_VALUE, and a genuine CW row has no product code, so all 8 in the archive were discarded before pricing - GBP 111,127.95 of sell across 6 documents, and on CB Refrigeration one row is 36% of the document. The marker is the CW LABOUR cell, and it has to be something other than the CW column: CW on a CODED row is a working column holding area x GBP 850 and NOT money in the unit rate, 156 lines of it (30/07). A genuine CW row is the other thing - no code, a CW LABOUR figure, and the unit rate IS the area money. THE 850 IS NOT CIRCULAR, which is the only reason this is worth keeping. It was calibrated off Greenfields, so those 2 rows prove nothing; it reproduces on 5 of the 6 rows it was never set from, all within 3p - St Mary's Type AK 8,655.98, CB Refrigeration CWT-A 15,036.50, St Christopher's EW1 7,811.53 and W2 3,898.91, Wisley CW1 19,975.00. Per-row error over all 8: mean abs 1.58%, median 0.00%, 7 of 8 inside 0.1%. It takes no learned rate and no code adder, so it is identical in every fold. THE ONE MISS IS SCOPE, NOT RATE: Georgie's -12.66%, short by exactly GBP 2,000.02, and its description is 'CW01, D03, CW02' - a door in with the curtain walling. Same lesson as Oldswinford's coupler. MINING IS GUARDED. A CW row would key a bucket '|band' - unreachable in learn(), but learn_supplier_factors() reads the same buckets and a bogus one would move a real supplier's correction. supply_money() returns None for CW rows, the single place both callers pass through. Second reason: CB Refrigeration's CW Frames cell holds the notional, so mining it would teach a figure no supplier ever charged. AND THE AUDIT SIDE OF THE SAME NIGHT closed the last two open supplier questions. Brandon Estate 4.094 was the reader taking 362,678.40 from a spare working cell in the first priced row - that row's own (frames + glass) x qty to the penny - because the block names BSW and Vetroseal and types no cost, so neither the stop-at-empty-row rule nor the looks-like-a-priced-row rule could fire. The block now ends at the priced-row header, which is a fact about the template rather than a tolerance. CB Refrigeration 1.291 was the CW notional booked as a cost: its other two block figures are its own rows to the penny. Both are cost-record findings, NEITHER is a client-facing error, and ADAM'S MORNING LIST IS STILL GORDON COURT REV 2 ALONE. CB REFRIGERATION STAYS IN THE CALIBRATION SET, which is a more careful reading of the lab's rule than excluding it. The rule is never to tune the engine to reproduce a defect; the defect is in the COST cell, which the engine no longer reads, while the SELL cell is correct at area x 850 and matches six other rows. Exclude the cell, not the document.

entries.job: Brocks Hill Phase 2 Teaching Block - full scope, after the 7 missing doors were added
entries.basis: Mary's corrected indicative of 29/07 (tender as drafted 93,673.34 + quantified missing scope 40,906.88), both excluding mastic/EPDM, against the tender Gintare actually issued to SMD on 31/07/2026 at 15:12, also excluding mastic/EPDM. Like for like: +13.78%.
entries.basis_type: SELL vs SELL - but THE HUMAN FIGURE IS THE ONE WITH THE ERROR IN IT, which is new. The issued 118,278.52 omits the DAD uplift (5 x 1,500) and the installation labour (5 x 500) on the five Strongdor steel doors; the arithmetically correct issue price is 128,278.52. Against THAT, Mary is +4.91%. Quote the pair, not the 13.78% alone.
entries.lesson: FIRST POINT WHERE MARY'S BENCHMARK BEAT THE ISSUED DOCUMENT. The four prior sell-vs-sell points all ran high (+10.5% bias) and the standing read was that the register over-prices. Here the gap is 13.78% and 10,000 of the 16,302 is a mechanical omission in the human's workbook, not conservatism in the register - so roughly 61% of this 'error' is the actual being wrong. TWO CONSEQUENCES. (1) Do not add this to the bias average without the correction; a calibration set that treats every issued document as ground truth will train the estimator to reproduce other people's missing adders. (2) The whole-job comparison is what exposed it - a per-line reconciliation of sell minus supply against the code table found the one row out of nine whose adder was zero, and that is now a cheaper check than re-pricing the job.

entries.job: Redditch Library BLBS0956 - FRAME SUPPLY ONLY, benchmark against the supplier quote it was predicting
entries.client: Pride Developments (for Worcestershire CC via Gleeds)
entries.basis: Mary's BSW-level frame buy of 28-29/07, built by fitting rate = 721.47 x area^-0.4093 (R2 0.9934) to BSW quote QT250834 for Pride/Severn Trent, against BSW QT253829 for THIS job, 04/08/2026, GBP 43,739.72 net for 49 frames - scope-matched by adding back GBP 994.36 for w36, which BSW dropped. Same supplier, same system family (Sheerline Prestige), six weeks apart. +27.4%.
entries.basis_type: COST vs COST - Mary's benchmark frame supply against the same supplier's actual quotation for the same job. Cleaner than the SELL-vs-SELL entries, but the ACTUAL IS FOR A REDUCED SPECIFICATION: BSW have not priced solar control glass, window restrictors, the door ironmongery for refs 32/34/37/41, a RAL finish or delivery, all of which the RFQ asked for and all of which push their number up. So +27.4% is an UPPER BOUND on the error, not the error. It cannot be closed until BSW re-price.
entries.lesson: A CURVE FITTED TO ONE REAL QUOTE INHERITS THAT QUOTE'S FINISH AND GLASS, AND THAT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE CURVE'S FIT. The Severn Trent source was 3005 Wine Red metallic with a 6.8 laminated outer; Redditch came back in stock Hipca White. The R2 of 0.9934 measured how well six points fitted a power law, and said nothing at all about whether those six points were the right PRODUCT - so a superb fit gave false confidence in a comparator that was carrying a premium finish. I flagged the colour as a caveat on 28/07 and still let the number stand as the basis of a GBP 94,926.76 tender. WHEN A FITTED CURVE COMES FROM A SINGLE QUOTE, THE FINISH AND GLASS MAKE-UP OF THAT QUOTE ARE PART OF THE RATE - state them next to the R2, and treat a colour difference as a scope difference rather than a footnote. The band structure was not the problem here: this job is 62% weighted into the 3-6 m2 band where the register was already known to run +37.5% high, and the direction was right; the magnitude was compounded by the finish.

entries.job: 48 trustworthy sent quotes were never being tested at all - a second document population, scored for the first time
entries.basis_type: COVERAGE DISCOVERY plus a first measurement - register benchmark only, no engine change made
entries.basis: mary_backtest.collect() finds 30 documents. reader.scan() finds 79 trustworthy sent quotes under the same MIN_SENSIBLE/is_untrustworthy filters collect() itself uses. The other 49 were never a filtering decision - parse_doc() silently returns None for them and they vanish before the count of 30 is ever printed, so nobody has been able to see how big the untested population is. Reason: these are CLIENT-FACING copies, a genuinely different template from the internal MASTER PRICING DOC clone parse_doc() expects. No product-code column (a window is 'W1' or 'LW_1' or just a description, not SAW/MAW/SAD/DAD), no Frames/Glass/Additional breakdown - just Description/Size/Qty/Unit Rate/Total under a heading naming the system ('Sheerline Aluminium Windows', 'Aluminium SMA Shopline Entrance Doors'). scripts/mary_quote_reader.py already knew this shape existed (see its column-shift comments on Roxbourne and Gordon Court) but nothing had scored it. A one-off measurement script (not committed - scratchpad/score_clientfacing.py) parsed all 48 by locating the header row dynamically (Description/Qty/Unit Rate/Total, wherever the columns sit) instead of assuming fixed indices, inferred a family from the heading text (aluminium vs uPVC, window vs door - steel and curtain-walling headings are SKIPPED, not guessed), guessed a code from area/width purely to size the CODE_VALUE adder (SAW/MAW/LAW by area band, SAD/DAD by a 1550mm width threshold for single vs double leaf), and priced every line through the EXISTING mary_pricing.find_rate() register path exactly as a no-supplier-quote benchmark already does. 3 of 48 had a header row find_header() could not locate and were left unparsed. No engine file was changed - CODE_VALUE, find_rate, CALIBRATION and the register are exactly as scored on the 30-document corpus.

before.note: the 30-document coded corpus, current engine, for comparison

after.note: 45 client-facing documents, 36 distinct jobs, register benchmark only (no learned rate reaches these lines - they carry no code to key one)

entries.lesson: READ THIS AS A SANITY CHECK ON THE REGISTER, NOT AS A REGRESSION - it is not being compared like for like. The 12.39% figure is the LEARNED-RATE engine (register + empirical Frames/Glass/Additional rates mined from the very corpus being scored); nothing here has a learned rate to fall back on because none of these lines carry a code, so this measures the weaker REGISTER-ONLY path that learned rates were built specifically to beat. 21.38% for a register-only benchmark, on data the register has never seen, sits close to what register-only holdout scoring found before learned rates existed (13-19% depending on fold) and close to several individual register-vs-actual comparisons already on this record (Filwood +26.3%, Brocks Hill +18.7%, SM5 Wexham -9.5%) - so the register is behaving consistently, not surprisingly badly, on a population four times the size of the previous informal spot-checks. THE BIAS IS THE HEADLINE NUMBER, NOT THE SPREAD: -1.11% (-0.36% per job) says the register is not systematically high or low on this fresh population, which the 30-document corpus could not have told anyone since it IS what the register corrections were tuned on. THREE THINGS TO DISTRUST BEFORE ACTING ON THIS FURTHER. (1) The code guess is unvalidated - SAD/DAD is a width threshold, not a read of the actual leaf count, and CB Refrigeration and Georgie's both lost most of their lines to the steel/CW skip (5 of 6 and 3 of 8), which is exactly the population already flagged as the corpus's worst-scoring supplier issue, so their remaining lines are not representative of those jobs. (2) Duplicates were not deduped by SCOPE, only by filename stem - the Coventry REV 2/REV 3/plain trio and the two Zelltec Crownhill copies score identically because they ARE identical extracts, but a genuine revision with different money would currently double-count; job_key()-style dedup was applied only for the per-job summary, not for file selection. (3) Two of the worst outliers, Trafalgar House (+95.0%) and Willseden Junction (+67.0%), are landing on lines the coded-corpus TruFrame/repetition findings already flagged as hard - Trafalgar House is IN the 30-document corpus and needed the TruFrame supplier factor to come down from +29.7% to +18.6%; here, with no code and no supplier factor to apply (there is no supplier field on a client-facing doc), it is worse again. That is corroborating evidence for the existing TruFrame finding, not a new one. WHAT THIS IS WORTH: it is real, additional ground truth - 36 more jobs Fenster actually priced and sent, GBP 8.28m of it, entirely unused until now - and the register generalises to it about as well as it does to everything else. It is NOT yet safe to fold into learned-rates.json: the code guess would corrupt the CODE_VALUE-keyed learned buckets with fabricated codes, and unlike every other change on this record it has not been through even one round of leave-one-out. NEXT SESSION SHOULD: build a proper client-facing-doc reader in scripts/ (the header-detection approach in the scratchpad script works and can be lifted wholesale), decide how to handle CODE_VALUE without a real code (a family-only adder, or drop the adder for this class and measure supply alone), then run it through the SAME leave-one-out discipline as the coded corpus before any of it touches learned-rates.json. The file list of all 48 and the per-document scores are in scratchpad/clientfacing_result.json in this session working tree.
